paras: The Webb City saloon stabbings were a knife attack on two Black men, Thomas Bettes and Mack Richardson, by two white men, Berry Harwood and George Hughes, in a saloon at Webb City, Arkansas, on the night of Saturday, September 24, 1881. Bettes died within a few hours and Richardson was stabbed in the breast; Harwood was captured while Hughes escaped. A Little Rock dispatch calling it 'a horrible butchery' was reprinted across the country, and the Chicago Tribune described the killings as 'entirely unprovoked'.

According to the Little Rock dispatch of September 27, Bettes and Richardson went into a saloon at Webb City, Franklin county, where a number of men had gathered, some of them drunk. Harwood and Hughes approached the two men, drew knives and "commenced carving." Harwood stabbed Bettes in the forehead and stomach, and Hughes stabbed Richardson in the breast. Bettes, the Memphis Appeal's version added, lived just long enough to point out Harwood before he died.

Harwood was captured, while Hughes escaped and was reported still at large. No report of an inquest, an indictment or a trial of either man appears in the coverage, nor any later word on Richardson's condition.

The story reached most papers as a single Little Rock wire dispatch, which ran on September 28 in the St. Paul Daily Globe under the head 'Arkansas Butchery', in the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer as 'A Horrible Butchery', and in the Gold Hill Daily News as 'Two Colored Men Butchered'. Western papers carried it over the following days, among them the Salt Lake Herald, the Sacramento Daily Record-Union and the Cheyenne Daily Leader, which headed it 'A Saloon Row' and misprinted the town as 'Wells City'. Spellings of the names drifted from copy to copy, with Bettes appearing as Beltes and Betts and Richardson's first name as Mackay or Mackey.

Headline writers placed the blame on the attackers: the Memphis Appeal titled its copy the 'Butchery of a Couple of Negroes by a Pair of Drunken Roughs'. The Chicago Tribune's news brief called Harwood and Hughes "the murderers" and said the killings were 'entirely unprovoked', a phrase the Superior Times repeated in early October. A different note appeared in the Bolivar Bulletin's Arkansas column on October 13, which grouped the affair with another 'small cutting and killing scrape' and described the victims as 'disorderly drunken negroes'.

Reports differ on the toll: the wire dispatch says only Bettes died and gives Richardson's wound without reporting his death, while the Tribune brief and the Bolivar column say both men were killed. The wire, as the fuller account with each wound described separately, is the better evidence for one death. The wire also placed Webb City in Franklin county, whereas the Bolivar column placed it in Sebastian county and gave Harwood's first name as Perry.

reader.title: Webb City saloon stabbings
bases: Two named white men attacked two Black men with knives in a saloon (A1, A2); no mob, band or crowd took part, so the episode is an assault by individuals rather than a mob assault or lynching (A3, A14).

The Little Rock wire dispatch (A1, A2) and an Arkansas news column with different details of county and spelling (A14) agree that Harwood and Hughes stabbed two Black men at Webb City, though they differ on the county and on how many died.

accounts.label: Little Rock wire dispatch
accounts.gist: Two Black men entered a saloon where some men were drunk; Harwood and Hughes approached them with drawn knives, killing Bettes and stabbing Richardson; Harwood was captured, Hughes escaped.

accounts.label: Chicago Tribune news brief
accounts.gist: Both Black men were stabbed to death by the two white men, Harwood was arrested and Hughes was at large, and the killings were 'entirely unprovoked'.

accounts.label: Arkansas news column (Bolivar Bulletin)
accounts.gist: A 'cutting and killing scrape' at Webb City, Sebastian county, in which two 'disorderly drunken negroes' were killed by Perry Harwood and George Hughes.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Little Rock dispatch under headlines such as 'Arkansas Butchery' and 'A Horrible Butchery', naming the victims as 'colored' and the attackers as white.
The Memphis Appeal headlined the 'Butchery of a Couple of Negroes by a Pair of Drunken Roughs', and the Chicago Tribune called the killings 'entirely unprovoked' murders.
The Bolivar Bulletin's Arkansas column treated it as 'a small cutting and killing scrape' and called the victims 'disorderly drunken negroes'.

conflicts.note: The wire dispatch is the fuller report and gives each wound separately; the Tribune and Bolivar items are condensed briefs.
The wire dispatch and a later Arkansas news column disagree; neither gives more detail on the place.
